newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries at session lows on Yellen comments.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries at session lows on Yellen comments.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices traded at session lows at midday with securities after remarks by Federal Reserve Board Governor prompted the loss of early gains and pushed the market lower, market analysts said.
"The Yellen remarks did it. There are no ifs, ands or buts about it," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
"The decline was mostly a reaction to some comments made by Janet Yellen," said Dana Johnson, head of resesarch for First Chicago Capital Markets.

In an interview with Reuters, Fed Governor Yellen said the U.S. economy has entered "an inflationary danger zone" and that the Fed must be alert to the risk that could pose to continued economic expansion.

Yellen stressed that there were uncertainties regarding the economy but her comments suggested that she might be willing to support a small, quarter percentage point rise in short-term interest rates at the Fed's next policy meeting on September 24 to act pre-emptively against higher inflation.
"Yellen had been viewed by the market as someone who might be somewhat more reluctant to tighten, said Johnson.

"Instead, her comments seemed to suggest that she was open to thinking about tightening so the market has gone back to worrying about the possibility of a Fed tightening in the near term," said Johnson.
Flanagan concurred.

"Despite the fact that the market already felt that the Fed could tighten on September 24, when you see comments suggesting this possibility from a Fed governor... This is a shot across the bow. It causes a little bit of anxiousness."
Immediately after the Yellen remarks, the bond prices erased modest gains and dipped lower.
In late morning trade, the 30-year long bond was down 14/32, a little more than half a point below its session highs.
At 1228 EDT/1628 GMT, the bond was down 20/32 to 95-12/32, yielding 7.13 percent. It had been down as much as 22/32.
"People are just dumping," said Waldo Best, senior economist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd Government Securities Inc.
Best was more dubious about the impact of Yellen's comments on the market.
"It's very much a case of people booking profits that they've made in the last two or three days," he said.
But he added, "The market is obviously very skittish."

The rash of second-tier economic data that the market got at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT was expected to have little impact and that, especially when they were overshadowed by the Yellen comments, proved to be the case.

"I don't think the 10 o'clock data had an impact," said Johnson. "I took note of the modest rise in inventories at the wholesale level and that suggests to me that there's some potential for some inventory in the months ahead that would contribute to strength in the economy.
July wholesale inventories rose 0.1 pct, the government reported, after rising 0.2 percent in June.

The upward revision in Q2 productivity to +0.5 pct "is exactly what one would have expected," said Johnson. "It was really an echo of the upward revision to second-quarter GDP. Likewise, the ($38.78 billion) current account deficit is a reflection of the growth in the trade deficit."
The Richmond Fed index rose in August but that, too, had no market impact, Johnson said.

At the short end of the maturity range, the three-month Treasury bill rate was up two basis points to 5.16 percent. The six-month and one-year bill rates were each up four basis points to 5.34 percent and 5.59 percent, respectively.

The two-year note was down 3/32 to 99-19/32, yielding 6.35 percent. The five-year note was down 8/32 to 99-3/32, yielding 6.72 percent, and the 10-year note was down 13/32 to 100-13/32, yielding 6.94 percent.
